name: On-Chain Governance
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Code That Votes on Itself
lesson.summary: On-chain governance encodes proposal submission, voting, and execution directly into a blockchain's smart contracts, so a passed vote can trigger the protocol change automatically without a separate manual deployment step.
lesson.body:
On-chain governance takes the general problem of blockchain governance, introduced in the previous section, and tries to solve it with the same tool the blockchain already uses for everything else: smart contracts. Instead of debating a change on a forum and then hoping enough node operators manually install it, an on-chain governance system lets accounts, usually weighted by how many governance tokens they hold or have staked, submit proposals and cast votes as on-chain transactions. If a proposal clears a defined threshold, such as a minimum quorum and a majority in favor, the change can be executed automatically, often after a timelock delay, without any single party needing to push a manual software update.

Tezos is the clearest example of this design taken to its logical end. Tezos calls itself a self-amending ledger: token holders vote across several periods on proposed protocol upgrades, and an upgrade that passes all periods is automatically activated on the network at a preset block height, rewriting even core consensus rules without a hard fork in the traditional sense. Compound and Uniswap show a related but narrower pattern common in decentralized finance: holders of a governance token vote on proposals, and if a proposal passes, a timelock contract executes the encoded changes, such as adjusting a fee parameter or moving treasury funds, after a mandatory waiting period that gives the community a window to notice and react to a malicious or mistaken proposal.

The appeal of on-chain governance is that outcomes are unambiguous and auditable. Anyone can verify exactly how many tokens voted which way and confirm that the executed code matches what was actually voted on, because the vote and the execution are both on the ledger. This can reduce the kind of prolonged, opaque argument that characterized The DAO fork, since a proposal either clears its threshold on-chain or it does not, and there is no separate step where node operators can quietly refuse to adopt the result the way Bitcoin or Ethereum Classic holders did.

That same automatic execution is also the design's biggest weakness. Because voting power is usually proportional to token holdings, on-chain governance tends toward plutocracy: a small number of large holders, early investors, or exchanges holding customer tokens in aggregate can dominate outcomes that most token holders never see, let alone vote on. Turnout in many token-voting systems is low, which lowers the bar an attacker needs to clear to pass a self-serving proposal; a governance attack does not need to fool a person, it just needs enough borrowed or purchased voting power for the length of one vote, a materially different threat model than persuading a distributed community of node operators over months.

Because the voting and execution logic is itself a smart contract, on-chain governance inherits every risk that applies to smart contracts generally: a bug in the governance contract can be as damaging as a bug in the application it governs, and an upgrade mechanism that is too easy to trigger can turn a feature meant to keep the protocol adaptable into a single point of failure. Designing the threshold, quorum, and timelock parameters correctly is itself a security-critical exercise, not an afterthought layered on top of an already-secure base.
